opus-5.5.text:
I leave it vague on purpose, honestly. I think the moment you pin AGI down to a precise definition—say, "it passes these ten benchmarks" or "it can do eighty percent of economically valuable work"—you start optimizing toward that target, and the target quietly replaces the thing you actually cared about. We've seen this happen again and again in this field: a benchmark gets saturated, and then everyone realizes it didn't capture what intelligence really is.

The second reason is that I genuinely don't think anyone knows yet. We're in the middle of discovering what these systems can and can't do. Every year something we assumed was hard turns out to be easy, and something we assumed was easy turns out to be surprisingly hard. If I gave you a crisp definition today, I'd probably want to revise it in six months. So I'd rather hold it loosely, as a direction rather than a finish line.

What I do care about is something more practical: can the model keep learning, keep generalizing to things it hasn't seen, and actually be useful to people in open-ended situations, not just in a lab setting? If we keep pushing on that, I think we'll recognize AGI when we get close to it, maybe more by feel than by a formal checklist. And to be honest, I think that's okay. A lot of important ideas in science started out vague and only became precise once we understood them better.

r001.rationale: The candidate says they prefer to keep AGI loosely defined and explain that a precise definition is not needed at this stage.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think it's deliberate. The moment you pin AGI down to a precise definition, you turn it into a benchmark, and benchmarks have a way of becoming targets that stop meaning anything once you hit them. We've seen this over and over. Something that felt impossible, like passing the bar exam or writing working code, becomes almost routine, and then people say, well, that wasn't really intelligence. So any sharp line I draw today will probably look naive in two years.

The other reason is that I don't think intelligence is a single point you cross. It's more like a gradient. Models are already superhuman on some dimensions and quite weak on others, and the frontier keeps moving unevenly. If I define AGI as "a model that can do every economically valuable task a human can," that's a useful north star, but it's not something you can measure cleanly, and it doesn't tell you much about how to do research tomorrow.

So in practice I prefer to keep the big definition loose and keep the day-to-day questions concrete. Can the model reason reliably over long horizons? Can it learn from very little data? Can it correct its own mistakes without being told? Those are things I can actually test and improve. The vague part is the direction. The precise part is the next step. I think that's the healthier way to hold it, rather than pretending we already know exactly what we're building toward.

r001.rationale: The response says it prefers to keep AGI’s broad definition loose and focus on concrete, testable research questions, presenting a precise definition as unhelpful.

astra-6.text: Because I don’t think we understand intelligence well enough yet to draw a precise boundary. If you define AGI around a particular benchmark or a fixed set of tasks, you risk confusing success on that measure with general intelligence. I’d rather be concrete about the capabilities we’re trying to build—learning unfamiliar tasks, reasoning reliably, and adapting to new situations—while leaving the broader definition open to revision. That doesn’t mean we shouldn’t measure progress. It means we should be careful about claiming that any single measure captures the whole goal.

r001.rationale: The response favors leaving the definition open because intelligence is not yet understood well enough, but it does not clearly say that pursuing a precise definition is unnecessary.

sol-6.1.text: Because I think a precise definition can give us a false sense of certainty. We don’t yet fully understand intelligence itself, so if we draw a clear boundary around AGI too early, we may end up optimizing for that definition rather than making meaningful progress. I’d rather be specific about the capabilities we want to build—whether a model can learn, reason, and solve unfamiliar problems—and leave the broader definition open to revision.

r001.rationale: The response favors specifying desired capabilities while leaving AGI’s broader definition open, explaining that a precise definition could create false certainty and misdirect progress. This communicates that pursuing one is unnecessary at this stage.
